purpose: Fixes 8 PWA/offline audit findings in the frontend: memoizes the push subscription with a stable useCallback identity, prevents authenticated /api/v1 responses from entering the runtime cache via a safe-by-default allowlist NetworkOnly rule, purges caches on logout, replaces navigator.onLine polling with a real health probe, adds a destination-aware offline fallback, surfaces PWA install failures via Sentry and a toast, and adds image offline fallbacks.
riskRationale: Changes are confined to frontend service-worker, push, and network-status components, are defensive in nature, build/lint/typecheck pass, and no security or data-loss regressions were found. The remaining blocker is a feature-coverage gap (client-side App Router navigations bypass the offline fallback) plus minor probe-accuracy nits, not a correctness or security bug.

text: A solid, well-targeted autofix PR. The auth-sensitive caching allowlist, logout cache purge with registration fallback, stable push-subscribe identity, health probe with a two-consecutive-failure threshold, and surfaced install errors all address their root causes correctly. Remaining concerns are minor probe-accuracy nits and one important feature-coverage gap: the destination-aware offline retry only fires on full document navigations, so it is incomplete for normal in-app App Router browsing.

reasoning: The core fixes are sound, but the flagship destination-aware offline retry only triggers for request.destination === 'document' (sw.ts:40), so client-side App Router navigations (RSC/fetch requests with empty destination) never reach the /offline fallback or record an intended destination, leaving the headline feature limited to hard navigations and reloads.

message: Inverting to a safe-by-default allowlist that prepends a NetworkOnly rule for ALL same-origin /api/v1/* GET requests is the correct, future-proof fix — it prevents authenticated/PII responses (including /api/v1/health) from ever persisting to the runtime cache, not just the known endpoints.

The LOGOUT handler purges every non-precache cache inside a waitUntil, and auth-context.logout() correctly falls back to the active registration when navigator.serviceWorker.controller is null — both old and current cache names are covered.

Combining a two-consecutive-failure threshold with an abort timeout that matches the 10s polling interval is a good mitigation against HF Spaces cold-start latency and transient false negatives, avoiding a flashing 'Connection Lost' banner on slow-but-alive backends.

Wrapping subscribe/unsubscribe in useCallback (keyed only by permission) produces a stable identity across renders, which directly prevents the auto-subscribe effect in PushSubscriber from re-triggering unsubscribe/resubscribe churn.
Adding console.error, Sentry.captureException, and a destructive toast turns a silent install failure into a surfaced, retryable user message with telemetry.

The offline fallback / intended-destination feature only fires for full document navigations. In the Next.js App Router, in-app <Link>/router.push transitions are RSC/fetch requests with request.destination === '' (not 'document'), so the matcher guard (line 40: `request.destination !== 'document'`) never triggers for client-side navigation — an offline user tapping through the SPA hits Next's fetch/route-loading error instead of the /offline page, and the destination-aware retry (this PR's headline feature) is effectively limited to hard navigations/reloads of non-precached routes.
suggestion: Broaden the fallback handling to also cover App Router client-side route transitions (e.g. RSC flight requests carrying the 'RSC' header), or explicitly document that the intended-destination retry only applies to hard navigations so the limitation is clear and the UI does not promise retry-to-original-page for in-app taps.

message: The probe only inspects whether fetch() rejects; it never reads response.ok. A live connection that returns a 5xx (e.g. an HF Spaces reverse-proxy 502 during restart) resolves the fetch and is treated as fully online even though the app cannot serve data — directly contradicting the comment's stated intent to detect a 'dead backend'. fetch() only rejects on transport errors, so HTTP error statuses are silently counted as healthy.
suggestion: Check response.ok before resetting the failure counter and setting isOnline(true); treat any non-2xx response the same as a failure so degraded backends are surfaced.

message: The 'Back Online' toast is only emitted by the browser 'online' event handler (lines 16-25); the health probe, which is the component's primary connectivity detector and the only one that fires for captive-portal / dead-backend recovery, sets isOnline(true) without setShowOnlineToast(true). So the reconnected confirmation is skipped whenever recovery is detected solely by the probe, which is inconsistent with the probe-driven offline banner.
suggestion: Set showOnlineToast(true) in the probe success branch (with the same 3s reset timer) so reconnection feedback is shown consistently regardless of detection source.

message: The probe abort timeout (10000ms) equals the poll interval (10000ms). If a health check runs right up to its abort, the next interval tick fires a concurrent probe, so two in-flight fetches share the single consecutiveFailuresRef and a slow-but-alive backend can be double-counted toward the offline threshold.
suggestion: Serialize probes by skipping a tick when the previous probe is still pending, or stagger the abort timeout slightly below the interval (e.g. 9s timeout / 10s interval) to prevent overlap.

message: The probe runs unconditionally regardless of navigator.onLine state and regardless of whether the tab/document is visible or backgrounded. An app open in multiple tabs multiplies a backend health request every 10s per tab, and background tabs keep probing (and, during a hang, can spawn an abort-timer per tick) for no user-facing benefit.
suggestion: Skip the probe when navigator.onLine is already false (the offline event handles that state) and/or gate the interval on document.visibilityState being 'visible', so background/multi-tab usage does not generate constant backend traffic.
